target: AG1's claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove schedule-based barriers to voting for most people
objection: A federal holiday would not reliably eliminate schedule-based barriers, because private employers are not required by federal law to give paid time off, and retail/service workers—especially low-income workers—often still work on federal holidays or would lose wages if they took time off to vote.

target: AG1's claim that a national Election Day holiday is an effective primary turnout strategy
objection: Research indicates that making Election Day a holiday by itself is not an effective way to increase voter turnout compared with other voting-access reforms such as employer time-off requirements or automatic voter registration.

target: AG2's claim that lack of guaranteed paid leave means a holiday would not meaningfully reduce voting barriers
objection: Even without a legal requirement for paid leave, national holidays typically lead to school closures and reduced or altered work schedules, so a holiday would still create practical voting windows and reduce scheduling conflicts.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday fails because it does not guarantee paid time off
objection: The holiday can increase voting through civic motivation: framing voting as a celebration rather than a chore can elevate the importance of democracy and encourage participation even without paid-leave guarantees.

target: AG2's recommendation that state employer-time-off rules and automatic voter registration should replace a holiday
objection: Those alternatives do not fully substitute for changing the election-day calendar, because they do not directly remove the underlying conflict between Election Day and required school/work hours nationwide.

target: AG2's claim that automatic voter registration and employer time-off rules are more reliable solutions than a holiday
objection: State-by-state employer time-off rules are uneven and may not exist or be well enforced everywhere, while automatic voter registration does not change whether someone is required to work or attend school on Election Day; a national holiday more directly addresses the schedule conflict.

target: AG2's claim that international precedent does not support a holiday approach
objection: The fact that 27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays shows the approach is workable and already used in comparable democracies, so it is not inherently the wrong strategy.

target: AG1's claim that OECD precedent shows election holidays are workable and effective
objection: Private employers in the U.S. are not required to close or provide paid leave on federal holidays, and many retail/service jobs still operate, so the existence of holiday-based elections elsewhere does not mean a U.S. federal holiday would solve low-income workers' access problems.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday would materially help low-income workers
objection: Because federal holiday status does not force private employers to close or provide paid leave, low-income workers in retail and service jobs would still face wage-loss and scheduling barriers, so the holiday would not reliably improve their voting access.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday is not workable because other countries use weekends/holidays differently
objection: A broad international pattern of holding elections on weekends or holidays indicates that the policy is institutionally workable and directly targets the schedule conflict that keeps millions of Americans from voting.

target: AG2's claim that low-income workers would still be blocked because schools and workplaces might not fully close
objection: For low-income parents, school closures on a holiday reduce childcare and school-day obligations, and many licensed childcare providers can operate during school-closure periods, so the holiday can materially reduce the childcare/school schedule barrier.

target: AG1's claim that school closures and reduced work schedules would sufficiently solve access barriers for low-income parents
objection: Low-income parents may still need affordable childcare or caretaking during voting hours, and school closure does not guarantee that substitute childcare will be available or affordable, so the holiday can leave the childcare barrier intact or just shift it.

target: AG2's assumption that substitute childcare will not be broadly available and affordable on Election Day
objection: The U.S. Child Care and Development Fund helps low-income working parents pay for childcare, and licensed providers commonly offer care when schools are closed, so substitute childcare could plausibly be available and affordable on a holiday Election Day.

target: AG1's claim that reduced school/work schedules would help low-income workers even without guaranteed paid leave
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to close or provide paid time off, so many low-income workers would still be scheduled to work and would still face wage loss if they took time to vote.

target: AG2's claim that reduced work/school overlap still would not help because private employers can keep workers on the job
objection: Federal holidays generally lead to school closures and reduced or altered staffing at many workplaces, so the overlap between required work and voting hours would still be reduced for many workers, including low-income shift workers.

target: AG1's claim that reduced overlap alone would meaningfully lower the voting burden for low-income workers
objection: Voting can take multiple hours for travel, waiting, and filling out a ballot, so even if a holiday reduces some overlap with work or school, low-income workers may still need unpaid time off and could still face wage loss or missed work.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday would reliably reduce barriers for low-income shift workers
objection: In retail and service jobs, holiday staffing often means some workers still work on the holiday, and without guaranteed paid leave they can still face wage-loss or missed-work pressure when voting, so the holiday does not reliably remove the barrier.

target: AG2's claim that shift workers would still face the same barrier because employers can keep them working
objection: Holiday staffing typically involves reduced or altered schedules, so the holiday would reduce the amount of time low-income shift workers are required to work during voting windows and thereby lower their wage-loss or missed-work pressure.

target: AG1's claim that reduced holiday staffing makes the policy reliable for low-income workers
objection: Employers can meet holiday demand by redistributing coverage rather than giving any particular worker guaranteed time off, and federal holiday status does not require paid leave, so low-income workers may still have to work during voting hours and face wage loss.

target: AG2's claim that holiday status does not reliably help low-income voters
objection: Because federal holidays typically cause school closures and reduced work schedules for many workplaces, the policy meaningfully reduces the schedule conflict for a broad share of low-income shift workers, making it a reliable primary way to lower those barriers.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday is only symbolic and not a serious reform
objection: A national Election Day holiday does more than symbolize civic participation: it reduces the central schedule-based access barrier and also increases civic motivation by making voting feel like a celebration, so it can function as a substantive turnout reform.

target: AG1's claim that a national Election Day holiday would reliably improve access for low-income voters because schools/workplaces would reduce obligations
objection: Private employers are not required to close or provide paid time off on federal holidays, retail and service work often continues, and low-income parents still may lack affordable substitute childcare, so the holiday would not reliably remove the work/wage or childcare constraints that actually block voting.
